title: Parvati's fire
hookLine: Parvati gives up even leaves in her tapas for Shiva, and the second limb turns to how you keep yourself

cards: Parvati, daughter of the Himalaya, has set her heart on Shiva, and Shiva sits in meditation, unmoved. So, in the poet Kalidasa's telling, she puts away her jewels and goes into the mountains to do tapas.

In summer she sits between four fires with the sun blazing overhead. In winter she stands in icy water. She lives on fallen leaves, then gives up even those, and people call her Aparna, the one without even a leaf.
One day a young ascetic arrives, sits down beside her, and starts to make fun of Shiva.

teach.b: He's smeared with ash, the visitor says. He wears snakes, haunts the cremation ground, rides an old bull. Why waste yourself on him?
Parvati flushes, defends Shiva, and gets up to leave. And the visitor takes his true form.
It was Shiva all along. From today, he tells her, I'm yours, bought by your tapas. Tapas means heat, and it sits at the center of today's limb.

teach.h: THE SECOND FIVE: HOW YOU KEEP YOURSELF.
teach.b: Sutra 2.32 names the niyamas, the observances: how you keep yourself, where the yamas face other people. Shaucha, cleanliness, outer and inner. Santosha, contentment.
Tapas, discipline, which the classical commentary describes as bearing the pairs: hunger and thirst, heat and cold. Svadhyaya, study, or repeating a mantra like Om.
And ishvara-pranidhana, offering everything you do to God.

The last three, discipline, study, surrender, are the same three Patanjali gave at the start of book two: kriya yoga, the practice for people who aren't born calm. Now notice what Parvati's heat is for.
It isn't punishment, and it isn't a show. It's devotion, lived in the body.
That's why, in many Hindu homes, people keep fasts: on Mondays for Shiva, on Ekadashi for Vishnu, and many women keep the Teej fast, which remembers Parvati's tapas. A fast like that isn't a diet.

how: In many Hindu homes and yoga lineages, the niyamas shape daily life: bathing before worship, fasts such as Monday fasts for Shiva, Ekadashi for Vishnu or the Teej fast that remembers Parvati, reading scripture or repeating a mantra, and offering one's actions to God; the young, the old and the unwell are usually excused from fasting.

o: five vows taken only by monks and nuns
five daily rituals done only at a temple
five observances for how you keep yourself

games.q: the five niyamas — tap the pairs.

s: the last three niyamas repeat kriya yoga from 2.1
discipline, study and surrender: the same three that opened book two.
in Kalidasa's telling, Parvati's tapas wins Shiva
the visitor who mocks Shiva turns out to be Shiva, who says he's hers, bought by her tapas.
tapas in the niyamas means punishing yourself
the commentary calls it bearing the pairs, hunger and thirst, heat and cold; in Parvati's story the heat is devotion.

games.q: your grandmother fasts every Monday but still cooks a full meal for everyone. by Parvati's story and 2.32, what is the fast?
o: a diet she happens to keep on Mondays.
tapas: discipline offered to Shiva, as Parvati's was.
a punishment for something she did.
games.why: tapas means heat. sutra 2.32 makes it one of the five observances, and in Parvati's story the heat is devotion, not punishment.

practice: Give this sit a little heat: stay still through one itch or one urge to check your phone, without fighting it.

Then touch the rest of the five lightly: a clean, cool breath, contentment with this seat, a slow Om or a name of God you love, repeated in your mind. If you pray, offer the sit to God. If you don't, simply let go of trying.

wordCard.voice: Niyama. The observances, the second limb of yoga: cleanliness, contentment, discipline, study and surrender to Ishvara.

orig.note: Sanskrit niyama: observance, rule; the second limb of yoga, after yama, restraint.

carryVoice: Your line: tapas, discipline offered to God. Parvati's heat wasn't punishment; it was devotion. Day four fifty-nine, done.
